Fabricius <note>Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, a Roman consul famous for his integrity and refusal of bribes</note>, a man of upright and sublime spirit, certainly felt this when he replied that he would rather rule over the rich than be rich himself. And indeed, for one person to overflow with pleasure and delights while others all around are groaning and lamenting is not the part of a kingdom, but of a jailer. Furthermore, just as a physician is most unskilled if he does not know how to cure a disease except by another disease, so he who does not know how to correct the life of citizens by any other way than by taking away the comforts of life, let him confess that he does not know how to rule over free men. Instead, let him rather change his own sloth or his pride, for it is usually by these vices that a people either despises him or holds him in hatred. Let him live harmlessly on his own, adapt his expenses to his income, restrain wickedness, and by the right instruction of his subjects, let him prevent rather than allow crimes to grow which he must then punish. Let him not rashly revive laws that have been abolished by custom, especially those that have long been discontinued and were never missed. Nor should he ever, under the name of a penalty, take anything of a sort that a judge would not allow a private citizen to take, as being unjust and crafty. Here, if I were to propose to them the law of the Macarensians <note>original: "Macarensium"; a fictional people located near Utopia</note> <margin>A wonderful law of the Macarensians</margin>, who also are not very far distant from Utopia; their king, on the first day he enters upon his reign, is bound by an oath after great sacrifices have been performed, that he will never have more than a thousand pounds of gold in his treasury at one time, or as much silver as would equal the value of that gold.
